rv.q: With an impeccable cast headed by Jesse Williams, Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Patrick J. Adams, Take Me Out just might be a revelation even to those who saw the original Broadway production nearly 20 years ago.
The comedy-drama has been buffed to a scintillating sheen by director Scott Ellis and his lineup of pro designers.
Richard Greenberg's must-see autopsy on baseball
Directed by Scott Ellis, it remains provocative, intelligent and engaging.
The long-awaited revival of Richard Greenberg's baseball play is a blunt, impactful, and humorous exploration of what it means to live your truth.
I believe that that will be your takeaway from when you go to see it and I urge you that you should as it is a wonderful piece of theater.
Nonetheless, “Take Me Out” proves to be the highlight of the current theatrical season, thanks to Greenberg, Ellis and a uniformly superb cast who consistently hit it out of the proverbial park.
Take Me Out also offers a vision of inclusion, of finding a place, finding friendship, and finding a home.
Take Me Out impresses again with its wit, wisdom, and lyrical appreciation of baseball.
This convincingly-acted, blistering drama more than earns its championship title.
Scott Ellis’s staging is brisk and effective, David Rockwell’s sets impressionistically evoke Yankee Stadium, and Bray Poor’s sound design plays amusingly with the sounds of the ballpark.
Scott Ellis’ production for Second Stage gets the maximum energy out of its shocking story.
Ferguson looks like he's having a lot of fun playing him, and his performance translates into a great time at the theater — something we could all use right now.

What’s truly impressive is the number, variety and depth of variations on the theme of personal identity that the author manages to coherently weave into his tale, most of which are successfully realized in Scott Ellis’ revival at the Theater under the aegis of Second Stage.
Richard Greenberg's skills both as a dramatist and a humorist, and especially as a master of repartee and wordplay.
Under the uneven direction of Scott Ellis, Take Me Out becomes a cluster of both remarkable and insignificant performances pieced together inside a scattered plot.
Suavely performed, this new production doesn’t add all that much substance to the conversation.
The latter is a silly sitcom about trivial stereotypes.
In mapping the existential gap between player and team, between person and tribe, Take Me Out was ahead of its time — and still is.

cn.t: Critics praise this Tony-winning revival as a powerful, entertaining exploration of identity and belonging that feels even more resonant 20 years later, anchored by strong performances and Greenberg's witty, lyrical writing.

vs.sum: The Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although some side seats may have partial views. The sound quality is generally strong, enhancing the theatrical experience. However, the seating is tight, which can affect comfort, particularly for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is charming with its historic character, and while facilities are adequate, expect some lines at the bar and restrooms.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
